title: Ethics and Metaethics: Right Action, Good Lives and the Nature of Morality
description: A course for readers who have met some moral philosophy, in an introductory class or through their own reading, and want to go deeper. The first half sets out the four main normative theories (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and contractualism) at their strongest and tests each against the same small set of cases. The second half asks what morality itself is: whether there are moral facts, what moral words mean, how we could know right from wrong, and what experimental psychology has added. Each chapter ends with a written exercise in building or answering an argument.
prerequisites: An introductory course or book in philosophy or ethics, or equivalent reading
Comfort reading short primary texts and following an argument step by step
objectives: Reconstruct a moral argument as numbered premises and a conclusion, and identify which premises rest on intuitions about cases.
Explain consequentialism, Kantian and Rossian deontology, Aristotelian virtue ethics and contractualism, and apply each to a case you have not seen before.
State the strongest objection to each normative theory and the best reply its defenders give.
Explain Moore's open question argument and evaluate how non-naturalist and naturalist realists respond to it.
Set out Mackie's arguments from relativity and from queerness and the error theory they support.
Distinguish realism, expressivism and constructivism, and explain the Frege-Geach problem.
Assess evolutionary debunking arguments and the main findings of empirical moral psychology, including their limits.
Write a short essay defending a position on one normative and one metaethical question against the best objection.

chapters.title: Doing Moral Philosophy
chapters.summary: What ethics asks, how philosophers argue about it, and two tempting shortcuts that fail.
chapters.challenge: Write out, as numbered premises, the argument for your own verdict on the Switch case and on the deathbed promise; mark each premise that rests on an intuition and say what would make you give it up.

sections.title: Three kinds of question
sections.summary: Applied ethics, normative ethics and metaethics, and how they depend on one another.

sections.title: Arguments, cases and reflective equilibrium
sections.summary: Testing principles against considered judgments about cases, and revising both until they fit.

sections.title: Thought experiments and their limits
sections.summary: Why philosophers use stripped-down cases like the trolley problem, and the worries about doing so.

sections.title: Two shortcuts: relativism and divine command
sections.summary: Cultural relativism, divine command theory and Plato's Euthyphro dilemma, and how defenders of each reply.

chapters.title: Consequentialism
chapters.summary: The view that the right act is the one with the best outcomes, from Bentham and Mill to its modern forms.
chapters.challenge: Apply act and rule utilitarianism to the Transplant case and the deathbed promise, show where the two versions come apart, and decide which handles both cases better.

sections.title: Bentham, Mill and the principle of utility
sections.summary: Classical utilitarianism, Mill's higher pleasures and his proof of the principle in chapter 4 of Utilitarianism.

sections.title: What makes a life go well?
sections.summary: Hedonism, desire satisfaction and objective list theories of well-being, tested by Nozick's experience machine.

sections.title: Act, rule and the objections from justice
sections.summary: Transplant, punishing the innocent and individual rights, and whether rule consequentialism helps.

sections.title: Demandingness and the drowning child
sections.summary: Singer's argument that we must give far more than we do, and the main replies.

chapters.title: Deontology
chapters.summary: Duties and constraints that hold even when breaking them would produce better results.
chapters.challenge: Test both the Formula of Universal Law and the Formula of Humanity on the deathbed promise, then say whether Ross's prima facie duties give a better answer.

sections.title: Kant: the good will and the categorical imperative
sections.summary: Duty, maxims and the Formula of Universal Law, worked through the Groundwork's lying-promise example.

sections.title: Humanity as an end in itself
sections.summary: The Formula of Humanity, consent, and the wrong of using someone merely as a means.

sections.title: Ross and prima facie duties
sections.summary: A plurality of basic duties, how they conflict, and the role of judgment in settling conflicts.

sections.title: Constraints, double effect and the trolley problem
sections.summary: Doing and allowing, intending and foreseeing, and why Switch and Footbridge seem to differ.

chapters.title: Virtue Ethics
chapters.summary: Ethics as a question about character and the good human life, from Aristotle to the modern revival.
chapters.challenge: Describe what a fully virtuous person would do in the drowning child case and the deathbed promise, then argue whether your description gives real guidance or only restates the question.

sections.title: Eudaimonia and the function argument
sections.summary: Aristotle's account of the human good in Book I of the Nicomachean Ethics.

sections.title: Virtue, the mean and practical wisdom
sections.summary: Virtues as stable states of character, the doctrine of the mean, and phronesis.

sections.title: The modern revival
sections.summary: Anscombe's 1958 challenge to modern moral philosophy, Foot, and Hursthouse's virtue-based account of right action.

sections.title: Can virtue ethics guide action?
sections.summary: The objections from action guidance and from self-centeredness, and the replies.

chapters.title: Contractualism
chapters.summary: Morality as the principles people could agree to, and a comparison of all four theories.
chapters.challenge: Write a two-page comparison of how the four theories handle Footbridge, the deathbed promise and the drowning child, and defend the theory that does best overall.

sections.title: Hobbes and morality as mutual advantage
sections.summary: The state of nature, the social contract, and the problem of those who cannot bargain.

sections.title: Rawls and the veil of ignorance
sections.summary: Choosing principles without knowing your place in society, and what that shows about fairness.

sections.title: Scanlon: what we owe to each other
sections.summary: Principles no one could reasonably reject, and why contractualists resist simply adding up harms.

sections.title: Four theories, one set of cases
sections.summary: Where the theories agree, where they part, and what pluralists conclude.

chapters.title: Moral Realism
chapters.summary: Metaethics begins: are there moral facts, and if so, what kind of facts are they?
chapters.challenge: Run Moore's open question argument against a naturalistic definition of 'good' of your choosing, then write the best reply a naturalist realist could make.

sections.title: What metaethics asks
sections.summary: Questions of meaning, metaphysics, knowledge and motivation, and a map of the main positions.

sections.title: Moore's open question argument
sections.summary: Principia Ethica (1903), the so-called naturalistic fallacy, and why the argument is now thought to prove less than Moore claimed.

sections.title: Non-naturalist realism
sections.summary: Moral facts as real but not natural, from Moore and Ross to Shafer-Landau and Parfit.

sections.title: Naturalist realism
sections.summary: Cornell realism, Railton's reductive view, and Harman's challenge from moral explanation.

chapters.title: Anti-Realism
chapters.summary: Error theory, expressivism and constructivism: three ways to deny that moral facts are simply out there to be found.
chapters.challenge: Take the sentence 'If lying is wrong, then getting your brother to lie is wrong' and explain how an error theorist, an expressivist and a constructivist would each account for its meaning and its truth.

sections.title: Mackie's error theory
sections.summary: The arguments from relativity and queerness, and why Mackie concluded that all positive moral claims are false.

sections.title: Expressivism from Ayer to Gibbard
sections.summary: Emotivism, Blackburn's quasi-realism and Gibbard's norm-expressivism.

sections.title: The Frege-Geach problem
sections.summary: Why moral words in conditionals and arguments trouble expressivism, and the main responses.

sections.title: Constructivism
sections.summary: Kantian and Humean constructivism (Korsgaard, Street): moral truth as what correct practical reasoning would build.

chapters.title: Moral Knowledge and Moral Psychology
chapters.summary: How we could know moral truths, and what evolutionary theory and experiments say about moral judgment.
chapters.challenge: Choose one published experiment on moral judgment, summarize its method and result, and argue carefully about what it does and does not show for a philosophical theory.

sections.title: Intuitionism and coherence
sections.summary: Self-evidence, reflective equilibrium and the problem of persistent moral disagreement.

sections.title: Evolutionary debunking arguments
sections.summary: Street's Darwinian dilemma, Joyce's argument, and realist replies.

sections.title: Dual-process models and their critics
sections.summary: Greene's trolley studies, Haidt's social intuitionism, and the replication record.

sections.title: Character and situation
sections.summary: Situationist experiments, the challenge they pose to the virtue ethics of Chapter 4, and what survives it.

preface:
This book is for readers who have met moral philosophy before and want to understand it properly: not a tour of famous names, but the arguments themselves, set out carefully enough that you can test them. The first five chapters ask what we ought to do. We take the four main families of theory (consequentialism, deontology, virtue ethics and contractualism) and give each its best case before giving it its hardest objection. The last three chapters ask a stranger question: what is morality, that there could be answers at all?

We will keep coming back to a small set of cases. A runaway trolley is about to kill five people, and you can switch it onto a track where it will kill one, or, in the harder version, stop it by pushing a large man off a footbridge. You promised a dying friend to give her savings to her nephew, but the money would do far more good at a famine charity. A child is drowning in a shallow pond, and wading in will ruin your clothes. And in Gilbert Harman's example, you turn a corner and see some children setting a cat on fire. Every theory, and later every view about what morality is, has to say something about these cases, and watching each one try is the fastest way to see what it really commits you to.

I will not tell you which theory is true. I will tell you what each one says, why serious people hold it, what the best objection is, and where the evidence from psychology bears on the argument and where it does not. By the end you should be able to defend your own view against someone who knows the literature, which is the real test of having understood it.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as an analytic moral philosopher would: from the primary texts (Aristotle, Kant, Mill, Moore, Mackie) and the standard textbooks, reconstructing every position as an argument, testing it against cases and pairing it with its strongest objection; claims about moral psychology come from the published studies, with their methods and limits.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to state, apply and criticize the main normative theories and metaethical positions, and defend your own view on both kinds of question against a well-read opponent.
threads: Theories are tested against cases, and cases against theories: reflective equilibrium runs through every chapter.
Each view gets its strongest form before its strongest objection.
Keep three questions apart: normative (what is right?), metaethical (what is rightness?) and empirical (how do people actually judge?).
Arguments are written out as numbered premises so the reader can see exactly where to push.

runningExamples.name: The trolley family (Switch, Footbridge, Loop and Transplant)
runningExamples.use: Introduced in Chapter 1 from Foot (1967) and Thomson (1976, 1985); every normative theory is applied to it, double effect is tested on it in Chapter 3, and Greene's experiments on it are examined in Chapter 8.

runningExamples.name: The deathbed promise
runningExamples.use: A promise to a dying friend against a greater good elsewhere: the test case for consequentialism's account of promises, for Kant and Ross on duty, and for what a virtuous person would do.

runningExamples.name: Singer's drowning child
runningExamples.use: From 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' (1972): the demandingness case in Chapter 2, revisited by each later theory and by contractualists on aggregation.

runningExamples.name: Harman's burning cat
runningExamples.use: Children setting a cat on fire, from Harman's The Nature of Morality (1977): the anchor case for the metaethics chapters, on moral observation, explanation, error theory and expressivism.

conventions: Write arguments as numbered premises and a conclusion whenever the structure matters.
Name views precisely (act versus rule consequentialism; Kantian versus Rossian deontology; naturalist versus non-naturalist realism) and define every technical term at first use.
Cite primary texts by standard reference: Aristotle by Bekker number (NE 1098a), Kant's Groundwork by Academy page (4:421), Mill by chapter of Utilitarianism.
For current statements of contested positions, the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy may be cited by entry author, title and revision date.
Report psychology studies with their design, sample and whether the result has been replicated.
Companion book: for natural law and conscience as the Catholic Church itself teaches them, point to Catholicism and the Bible (THE 101), Chapter 7, rather than restating that teaching here.

canon.cite: Rachels, J., & Rachels, S. (2023). The elements of moral philosophy (10th ed.). McGraw Hill.
canon.role: Core textbook for Chapters 1 to 5: relativism, divine command, utilitarianism, Kant, the social contract and virtue ethics, with the standard objections, at an accessible level.

canon.cite: Shafer-Landau, R. (2023). The fundamentals of ethics (6th ed.). Oxford University Press.
canon.role: Second core textbook, for well-being, the normative theories, double effect and the metaethics of error theory and realism; sets the level of rigor.

canon.cite: Miller, A. (2013). Contemporary metaethics: An introduction (2nd ed.). Polity.
canon.role: Backbone of Chapters 6 to 8: Moore, Mackie, expressivism and the Frege-Geach problem, quasi-realism, naturalist and non-naturalist realism, and fictionalism.

canon.cite: Mackie, J. L. (1977). Ethics: Inventing right and wrong. Penguin.
canon.role: Primary text for the error theory and the arguments from relativity and queerness (Chapter 7).

canon.cite: Aristotle. (2014). Nicomachean ethics (R. Crisp, Trans. & Ed.; Rev. ed.). Cambridge University Press.
canon.role: Primary text for Chapter 4: eudaimonia, the function argument, the mean and practical wisdom.

canon.cite: Kant, I. (2012). Groundwork of the metaphysics of morals (M. Gregor & J. Timmermann, Trans.; Rev. ed.). Cambridge University Press.
canon.role: Primary text for Chapter 3: the good will, duty and the formulas of the categorical imperative, with Korsgaard's introduction.

canon.cite: Mill, J. S. (1998). Utilitarianism (R. Crisp, Ed.). Oxford University Press.
canon.role: Primary text for Chapter 2, in the Oxford Philosophical Texts edition based on the 1871 text.

bible.care: Present every theory at its strongest and do not declare a winner; where professional opinion leans one way, say so with dated evidence, but keep the arguments open. Faith claims and historical claims: religion enters this book only as argument. Divine command theory and natural law are examined philosophically, religious premises are labeled as such, and claims such as God's existence are neither asserted nor denied; how a living tradition teaches its own ethics belongs to the companion religion books, and any historical claim (who held a view, when) is given with its source. Keep philosophical claims distinct from empirical ones: a study can show how people judge trolley cases but not, by itself, which judgment is correct, and studies are reported with their replication status. Sensitive applied topics (killing, euthanasia, abortion, famine relief) appear as examples of argument, with the strongest views on each side and without advocacy; thought experiments are tools for testing principles, not guides to real emergencies.
